prompt: A cable run passes close alongside several other active cables, and one pair's signal induces noise onto an adjacent pair within the same cable. What is this phenomenon called?
choices: Attenuation
Crosstalk
Latency
Collision
explanation: Crosstalk (near-end crosstalk, or NEXT) is signal bleed between adjacent wire pairs. Proper twisting of pairs is designed specifically to cancel this out; damaged or untwisted sections make it worse.

prompt: A fiber run measures a signal loss of 0.5 dB per kilometer, and the link fails once the run exceeds the transceiver's power budget. What is this signal weakening over distance called?
choices: Attenuation
Crosstalk
Jitter
A split pair
explanation: Attenuation is the gradual loss of signal strength as it travels down a cable, measured in dB. Every cable type has a maximum supported distance before attenuation exceeds what the receiver can reliably decode.

prompt: A newly terminated Ethernet cable links two devices, but the connection never comes up even though a link light is present on one end. A cable tester shows pins 1/2 and 3/6 swapped between the two ends. What is this fault called?
choices: TX/RX reversed
A short circuit
Attenuation
An open circuit
explanation: When the transmit and receive pairs are wired backward relative to each other, the two ends can't understand each other even if a physical link is detected. Straight-through cables must keep TX at one end aligned with RX at the other.

prompt: A cable tester reports infinite resistance on one conductor of a copper run, and the link never comes up at all. What kind of fault does this indicate?
choices: A short circuit
An open circuit (a break in the conductor)
Crosstalk
A duplex mismatch
explanation: An open circuit means the conductor is physically broken somewhere along its length, so no current or signal can pass — infinite resistance is exactly what an open shows on a continuity test.

prompt: Two conductors that should be separate are touching somewhere along a cable run, and a continuity tester shows near-zero resistance between wires that shouldn't be connected. What fault is this?
choices: An open circuit
A short circuit
Attenuation
A split pair
explanation: A short circuit occurs when two conductors that should be electrically isolated make unintended contact, which a tester reads as abnormally low resistance between them.

prompt: A workstation's connection drops intermittently whenever the cable is nudged near the wall plate, and visual inspection shows a cracked, poorly seated RJ45 connector. What is the most likely root cause of the intermittent connectivity?
choices: DHCP scope exhaustion
A damaged or improperly seated connector
DNS cache poisoning
MTU mismatch
explanation: A physically damaged or loose connector can make and break contact with slight movement, producing exactly this kind of intermittent, physically triggered disconnect.

prompt: A technician wants to run a single Cat6 segment 130 meters from the switch to a workstation with no intermediate equipment. What problem should be expected?
choices: None — copper Ethernet has no meaningful distance limit
The run exceeds the 100-meter maximum distance for standard copper Ethernet and will likely fail or perform unreliably
It will work but only at half the rated speed automatically
It will only be a problem if the cable is Cat5e instead of Cat6
explanation: Twisted-pair Ethernet standards specify a 100-meter maximum segment length (including patch cords). Beyond that, attenuation degrades the signal past what the receiver can reliably interpret, requiring a repeater, switch, or media conversion to fiber.

prompt: Which tool verifies that all eight conductors in a copper cable are wired straight-through and continuous, quickly flagging opens, shorts, and miswires?
choices: A cable tester (wiremap tester)
An OTDR
A tone generator and probe
A packet sniffer
explanation: A basic cable tester checks the wiremap and continuity of each pin end-to-end, which is the fastest way to confirm a newly terminated cable is wired correctly before it's put into service.

prompt: A copper cable tests as having a break, but the run is buried and its exact physical location is unknown. Which tool pinpoints the distance to the fault?
choices: A Time Domain Reflectometer (TDR)
A multimeter
A toner probe
A loopback adapter
explanation: A TDR sends a signal down the cable and measures the time it takes to reflect back off a fault, calculating the distance to the break so technicians can locate and repair it without digging up the entire run.

prompt: Which tool is the fiber-optic equivalent of a TDR, sending light pulses down a fiber strand to locate breaks and measure loss at each splice or connector?
choices: An OTDR (Optical Time Domain Reflectometer)
A cable certifier
A tone generator
A punch-down tool
explanation: An OTDR characterizes a fiber run's loss profile end-to-end and can identify the location of breaks, bad splices, or excessive bends by analyzing reflected and backscattered light.

prompt: A technician needs to identify which of dozens of unlabeled cables in a wiring closet corresponds to a specific wall jack. Which tool set is designed for exactly this?
choices: A tone generator and probe
An OTDR
A multimeter
A loopback adapter
explanation: A tone generator injects an audible signal onto a cable at one end, and the probe detects that tone at the other end, letting a technician trace a specific cable through a bundle or wall without visual continuity.

prompt: A technician wants to verify a switch port's transmit and receive circuitry is functioning without connecting it to another live device. What tool plugs directly into the port to test this?
choices: A loopback adapter
A tone generator
An OTDR
A packet sniffer
explanation: A loopback adapter wires the transmit pins directly back to the receive pins, letting a port test its own send/receive circuitry in isolation, without needing a second device on the other end.

prompt: A technician suspects a PoE switch port isn't delivering the expected voltage to an access point. Which basic tool measures voltage, continuity, and resistance directly?
choices: A multimeter
A protocol analyzer
A port scanner
An IPAM system
explanation: A multimeter measures electrical properties like voltage, current, resistance, and continuity, making it useful for verifying power delivery issues such as a PoE port not supplying the expected voltage.

prompt: Which command-line tool sends ICMP echo requests to test basic reachability and round-trip time to a host?
choices: ping
netstat
nslookup
arp
explanation: ping is the most basic connectivity test, sending ICMP echo requests and reporting whether replies come back and how long they take.

prompt: Which Windows command displays the full IP configuration of every network adapter, including IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers?
choices: ipconfig /all
netstat -an
nslookup
tracert
explanation: ipconfig /all shows complete adapter details. Plain ipconfig shows a shorter summary without DNS servers, MAC address, or lease information.

prompt: A workstation shows a stale DHCP lease and needs to give it up and immediately request a new one. Which pair of Windows commands accomplishes this?
choices: ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /flushdns then ipconfig /registerdns
netstat -r then netstat -e
nslookup then arp -a
explanation: ipconfig /release gives up the current DHCP lease, and ipconfig /renew immediately requests a fresh one from the DHCP server, which is useful when a client has a bad or stale address.

prompt: A technician wants to query a domain's MX records specifically, rather than its default A record, directly from the command line. Which tool supports this?
choices: nslookup
ping
arp -a
netstat
explanation: nslookup (or dig on Linux/macOS) can query specific DNS record types like MX, TXT, or NS, not just the default A/AAAA lookup, which is useful for troubleshooting mail flow or DNS delegation.

prompt: Which command lists all active TCP connections and listening ports on a local Windows machine?
choices: netstat -an
ipconfig /all
tracert
nslookup
explanation: netstat -an shows active connections and listening ports numerically, which helps identify unexpected open ports or unwanted outbound connections.

prompt: A technician wants both the hop-by-hop path to a destination and statistical packet loss/latency data at each hop over time, combined into a single tool. Which command provides this?
choices: pathping
ping -t
arp -a
ipconfig /all
explanation: pathping combines the hop discovery of tracert with extended statistics gathered over time at each hop, making it useful for spotting exactly where intermittent loss is occurring along a path.

prompt: Before deploying a new server, a security-conscious admin scans it from another host to see which TCP ports are open and responding. What kind of tool is being used?
choices: A port scanner
A tone generator
A TDR
An IPAM system
explanation: A port scanner probes a range of ports on a target host to determine which are open, closed, or filtered — useful both for attackers and for defenders auditing their own exposure.

prompt: A user complains that file downloads are much slower than their ISP's advertised plan. Which tool measures actual throughput to a distant test server for comparison?
choices: A speed test utility
arp -a
A cable tester
A loopback adapter
explanation: Speed test tools measure real-world upload and download throughput (and often latency) against a nearby test server, giving a practical comparison against the advertised or contracted bandwidth.

prompt: A wireless network in an office kitchen area experiences frequent dropouts whenever the microwave oven is running. What is the most likely cause?
choices: RF interference from the microwave on the 2.4 GHz band
A duplicate IP address
MTU mismatch
DNS cache poisoning
explanation: Microwave ovens, along with cordless phones and some Bluetooth devices, operate in or near the 2.4 GHz band and can cause significant interference to Wi-Fi on that band.

prompt: Two access points in adjacent rooms are both set to the same 2.4 GHz channel, and clients near the boundary experience poor throughput and retries. What is this problem called?
choices: Channel overlap / co-channel interference
MTU mismatch
A duplicate IP address
Asymmetrical routing
explanation: When neighboring APs share the same or overlapping channels, their signals interfere with each other, forcing more retransmissions and reducing throughput for clients in the overlap zone. Staggering non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11 on 2.4 GHz) avoids this.

prompt: Users at the far end of a warehouse report very weak or absent Wi-Fi signal, while users near the single access point have no issues. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Insufficient coverage — the AP placement and count don't adequately cover the whole space
A rogue DHCP server
An MTU mismatch
VLAN hopping
explanation: A dead zone at the far end of a large space typically means the existing AP or APs simply don't reach that area with sufficient signal strength — the fix is usually additional APs or better placement, informed by a site survey.

prompt: An access point is mounted flat against a metal ceiling duct, and coverage in the room below is noticeably worse than expected for its rated range. What is the most likely issue?
choices: Poor antenna placement, with a large metal obstruction blocking and reflecting the signal
A DHCP scope exhaustion
An open circuit in the Ethernet cable
A DNS resolution failure
explanation: RF signals are absorbed and reflected by metal. Mounting an AP against or near large metal surfaces significantly degrades coverage regardless of the AP's rated range.

prompt: An access point installed to cover a long hallway uses an omnidirectional antenna, and coverage trails off quickly at both ends of the hall despite adequate signal in the middle rooms off to the side. What would likely improve this?
choices: Replacing the omnidirectional antenna with a directional antenna aimed down the hallway
Lowering the AP's transmit power
Switching from WPA3 to WPA2
Changing the DHCP scope
explanation: An omnidirectional antenna spreads signal evenly in all directions, which wastes energy to the sides in a long, narrow space. A directional antenna focused down the hallway would concentrate coverage where it's actually needed.

prompt: A workstation can reach every other device on its local subnet but cannot reach anything beyond it, including the internet. Its IP configuration shows a gateway address that doesn't exist on that subnet. What is the likely cause?
choices: An incorrect default gateway
A duplicate IP address
DNS cache poisoning
Channel overlap
explanation: Local subnet traffic doesn't need a gateway, but anything destined off-subnet does. A wrong or unreachable default gateway address explains connectivity that works locally but fails everywhere else.

prompt: A user's laptop periodically loses network connectivity and Windows displays a warning that another device on the network is using the same IP address. What is the underlying problem?
choices: A duplicate IP address, likely from a static assignment conflicting with the DHCP scope
An MTU mismatch
A rogue DHCP server exhausting the scope
Asymmetrical routing
explanation: Two devices with the same IP on one segment will intermittently disrupt each other's connectivity, and Windows explicitly warns about this condition. It's commonly caused by a statically assigned address that overlaps with the DHCP scope.

prompt: A user can successfully ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot browse to any website by name, and pinging a website's name fails to resolve. What category of problem is this?
choices: A DNS resolution failure
A duplicate IP address
A cable open circuit
PoE power delivery failure
explanation: Reaching an IP address directly but failing on names points squarely at DNS — either the configured resolver is unreachable, misconfigured, or the record itself has a problem.

prompt: New devices on a large office subnet suddenly stop receiving IP addresses, while existing devices remain unaffected until their leases expire. What is the most likely cause?
choices: DHCP scope exhaustion — the pool of available addresses has been used up
A DNS cache poisoning attack
An OTDR misconfiguration
A native VLAN mismatch
explanation: If a DHCP scope runs out of free addresses, new lease requests simply can't be satisfied, while devices that already hold a valid lease keep working until it expires or is released.

prompt: A stateful firewall randomly drops legitimate sessions because outbound traffic leaves through one ISP link while the return traffic comes back through a different ISP link that never saw the original request. What is this routing condition called?
choices: Asymmetrical routing
A duplicate IP address
Channel overlap
A split pair
explanation: Asymmetrical routing happens when outbound and return traffic take different paths. Stateful devices like firewalls that only saw one direction of the conversation may treat the return traffic as unsolicited and drop it.

prompt: A video call has acceptable overall latency, but audio periodically stutters and cuts out because packet arrival times vary wildly from one moment to the next. What is this variation in delay called?
choices: Jitter
Attenuation
Crosstalk
Split pair
explanation: Jitter is the variation in packet delay over time. Real-time traffic like voice and video is especially sensitive to jitter, since inconsistent arrival timing disrupts smooth playback even when average latency looks fine.

prompt: During business hours, file transfers across the WAN link slow dramatically, and monitoring shows the circuit consistently running near 100% utilization at those times. What is this best described as?
choices: A bandwidth bottleneck
A duplicate IP address
DNS cache poisoning
A split pair
explanation: When a link's actual demand regularly approaches or exceeds its capacity, throughput for everyone sharing it degrades — a bandwidth bottleneck, typically resolved by upgrading capacity, adding a second path, or applying QoS.

prompt: After a VPN tunnel is deployed, small pings succeed but transfers involving large packets stall or fail silently, with no ICMP error returned because a device along the path has fragmentation-blocking rules. What is the likely cause?
choices: An MTU mismatch
A duplicate IP address
A wrong default gateway
Channel overlap
explanation: Tunneling protocols add overhead that can push packets past the path's maximum transmission unit. If ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages are blocked somewhere along the way, large packets are silently dropped instead of being fragmented or rejected with a clear error.

prompt: A workstation was moved to a new switch port that was accidentally left assigned to the wrong VLAN. What symptom would this most likely produce?
choices: The device gets an IP address (if the wrong VLAN also has DHCP) but cannot reach resources that live on its intended VLAN
The cable will show an open circuit on a tester
The switch port will show a duplex mismatch
The device will be unable to power on
explanation: An incorrect VLAN assignment is a configuration problem, not a physical one — the port and cable are fine, but the device ends up logically on the wrong segment, cut off from the resources and gateway it expects to reach.

prompt: When troubleshooting a connectivity problem using a bottom-up approach, place these OSI layers in the order they would be checked first to last.
explanation: A bottom-up approach rules out the simplest, most fundamental causes first — cabling and link status — before moving up through addressing, connections, and finally the application itself.

prompt: Type the Windows command that clears the local DNS resolver cache.
explanation: ipconfig /flushdns discards all cached DNS entries, forcing the next lookups to be resolved fresh — useful after a DNS record change or when a stale/poisoned entry is suspected.

prompt: An interface's error counters show a rising number of CRC errors on a copper link that was recently re-terminated. What does a CRC error MOST likely indicate here?
choices: Frames are arriving corrupted — typically bad termination, damaged cable, or interference
Frames are arriving smaller than the 64-byte minimum
Frames exceed the configured MTU
The port has been administratively shut down
explanation: A CRC error means the frame's checksum didn't match on arrival — the frame was corrupted in transit. After a re-termination, suspect the termination, cable damage, or interference. Undersized frames are runts; oversized are giants.

prompt: A switch port shows a status of 'err-disabled' after a user plugged in an unmanaged mini-switch. What should the technician do FIRST?
choices: Determine why the port was disabled (for example a port-security or BPDU guard violation) before re-enabling it
Immediately re-enable the port with no further investigation
Replace the switch
Increase the port's MTU
explanation: Err-disabled is a protective shutdown triggered by a specific violation — commonly port security or BPDU guard. Blindly re-enabling recreates the condition; identify the trigger first, which is also the methodology's 'identify the problem' step.

prompt: A newly installed PoE security camera fails to power on. Several other cameras on the same switch work normally. Which is the LEAST likely cause of this single camera failing?
choices: The switch's total PoE power budget is exhausted
The camera requires a higher PoE standard (for example 802.3at) than the port supplies
The patch cable to that camera is faulty
The camera itself is defective
explanation: An exhausted power budget usually affects newly added devices broadly and often logs a budget warning — but with several cameras already working and only this one failing, a port/cable/standard mismatch or a defective unit is far more likely than a switch-wide budget issue.

prompt: A technician must trace which physical cable in a crowded patch panel corresponds to a specific wall jack, then confirm the run has no opens or shorts. Which TWO tools are appropriate?
choices: Tone generator and probe
Cable tester
Protocol analyzer
Spectrum analyzer
NetFlow collector
explanation: A toner and probe identifies which physical cable is which; a cable tester verifies continuity, opens, shorts, and wire mapping. Protocol analyzers, spectrum analyzers, and flow collectors examine traffic or RF, not the physical cable path.

prompt: Following the troubleshooting methodology, which TWO actions belong to the FIRST step, 'identify the problem'?
choices: Question the user about what changed
Gather information and identify symptoms
Implement the permanent fix
Document the outcome
Verify full system functionality
explanation: Questioning users and gathering symptoms are both part of identifying the problem. Implementing, verifying, and documenting are later steps — jumping to the fix is the classic exam trap.

prompt: A fiber link is down between two buildings. Which TWO tools are appropriate for diagnosing the physical fiber run?
choices: An OTDR to locate a break by distance
A visual fault locator to reveal breaks or tight bends
A tone generator and probe
A multimeter set to measure resistance
A WiFi analyzer
explanation: OTDRs and visual fault locators are fiber-specific. Toners and multimeters are copper tools — fiber carries light, not current — and a WiFi analyzer examines RF.

prompt: Users on one VLAN cannot reach a server on another, though both hosts have correct addresses and can reach their own gateways. Which TWO should be examined?
choices: Access control lists filtering traffic between the two VLANs
The routing table and default routes on the Layer 3 device
The Wi-Fi passphrase on the guest network
The users' monitor resolutions
The printer spooler service
explanation: Both hosts reaching their gateways proves local addressing works, so the fault sits in inter-VLAN routing or a filter between them. Wireless credentials, displays, and print services are unrelated.

prompt: A user reports intermittent connectivity, and the switch port shows rising CRC errors and drops. Which TWO physical causes are MOST likely?
choices: A damaged or improperly terminated cable
Electromagnetic interference along the cable run
An expired user password
An incorrect default gateway
A full mailbox quota
explanation: CRC errors mean frames are arriving corrupted, which points to the physical path: bad termination or interference. Passwords, gateways, and mailbox quotas cannot corrupt frames on the wire.

prompt: A PoE camera fails to power on while others on the same switch work. Which TWO are plausible causes?
choices: The camera requires a higher PoE standard than the port supplies
The patch cable or port serving that camera is faulty
The switch has run out of VLAN IDs
The network's MTU is set to 1500
DNS resolution is failing for the camera's hostname
explanation: With other cameras working, the fault is specific to this device's power requirement or its physical path. VLAN IDs, standard MTU, and DNS have nothing to do with delivering power.

prompt: Following the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology, what must a technician do immediately after establishing a theory of probable cause?
choices: Test the theory to determine the cause
Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem
Implement the solution
Document findings, actions, and outcomes
explanation: Testing comes before planning: an untested theory can send you into a plan of action that fixes nothing. If testing disproves the theory, you return to establishing a new one or escalate.

prompt: A technician's theory about the cause of an outage is disproved by testing. According to the troubleshooting methodology, what are the two correct next options?
choices: Establish a new theory, or escalate the problem
Implement the original plan anyway and monitor the result
Document the findings and close the ticket
Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures
explanation: A disproved theory sends you back to the theory stage, or to someone with more expertise or access. Proceeding with a plan built on a theory you have already disproved is how small outages become long ones.

prompt: What is the final step of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?
choices: Document findings, actions, outcomes, and lessons learned
Verify full system functionality
Implement preventive measures
Establish a plan of action
explanation: Documentation is last, and it is the step most often skipped. It is also what turns a one-off fix into organizational knowledge the next technician can use.

prompt: A technician begins troubleshooting a failed application by checking whether the application service is running, then works down toward the physical link. Which approach is this?
choices: Top-down
Bottom-up
Divide and conquer
Substitution
explanation: Top-down starts at the Application layer and works toward the Physical layer, which suits problems where the physical infrastructure is known to be healthy. Divide and conquer starts in the middle, typically at Layer 3, and moves in whichever direction the evidence points.

prompt: During the identify-the-problem step, why does the methodology emphasise asking what recently changed?
choices: Because most faults follow a change, so recent changes are the highest-yield starting point
Because change records are required before any ticket can be opened
Because users are generally unreliable sources of information
Because changes must be reversed before troubleshooting can begin
explanation: A network that worked yesterday and fails today usually differs by something someone did. Checking the change log first frequently identifies the cause before any diagnostic tool comes out.

prompt: A 10 Gbps link between two switches will not come up. One end has a 10GBASE-SR transceiver on multimode fiber and the other has a 10GBASE-LR transceiver. What is the fault?
choices: A transceiver mismatch, since the two optics use different wavelengths and fiber types
A duplex mismatch between the two switch ports
An MTU mismatch preventing link negotiation
A VLAN mismatch on the trunk
explanation: SR optics use 850 nm over multimode and LR optics use 1310 nm over single-mode, so the two cannot interoperate even though both are 10 Gbps. Optics must match in speed, wavelength, and fiber type at both ends.

prompt: A new switch reports that a third-party transceiver is unsupported and keeps the port down, though the optic is physically correct. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The switch is enforcing vendor coding on the transceiver's EEPROM
The transceiver is rated for a longer distance than the fiber run
The fiber patch cable has reversed TX and RX strands
The port is configured with the wrong VLAN
explanation: Many vendors read an identification string from the optic and refuse modules that are not coded for their platform. The fix is either a vendor-coded optic or, on platforms that allow it, enabling unsupported transceiver support explicitly.

prompt: A switch has a 370 watt PoE budget. Nine access points drawing 30 watts each already run on it, and a tenth is added but never powers up, while the existing nine are unaffected. What has happened?
choices: The PoE power budget has been exhausted, so the newest device is denied power
The switch has run out of MAC address table entries
The tenth port has been placed in the wrong VLAN
Spanning tree has blocked the tenth port
explanation: Total PoE draw is limited by the switch's power supply, independent of what any single port can deliver. Switches generally allocate power in port order or by configured priority, so the last device added is the one left unpowered.

prompt: An IP phone requiring 802.3at power connects to a switch port that only supports 802.3af. What is the likely outcome?
choices: The phone either fails to power on or operates in a reduced-power mode
The switch automatically increases the port to 802.3at
The phone powers normally but negotiates half duplex
The port shuts down every other PoE device on the switch
explanation: 802.3af caps delivery at about 15.4 watts at the source, below what an at-class device requires. Powered devices signal their class during negotiation, which is why some degrade gracefully rather than failing outright.

prompt: A switch port's link LED is off entirely on both ends of a newly run cable, and the cable tests good. What should be checked next?
choices: Whether the port is administratively shut down or disabled
Whether the port's VLAN assignment is correct
Whether the DHCP scope has available addresses
Whether DNS resolution is working for the host
explanation: No link light at all means the problem is below Layer 3 — an administratively disabled port produces exactly this symptom with a perfectly good cable. VLAN, DHCP, and DNS issues all require a link to be established first.

prompt: A switch port shows a solid amber link LED rather than green. On most platforms, what does this typically indicate?
choices: The port is up physically but blocked by spanning tree or otherwise not forwarding
The port is negotiating at its maximum speed
The port is delivering PoE power correctly
The port has no cable attached
explanation: Amber conventionally indicates a link that exists but is not forwarding, most often because spanning tree has blocked it. LED conventions vary by vendor, which is why the documentation should be checked before drawing conclusions.

prompt: Users on a VLAN can reach servers on their own subnet, but a specific application on a remote subnet fails while ping to that same server succeeds. What is the most likely cause?
choices: An access control list is permitting ICMP but blocking the application's port
The default gateway is misconfigured on the client
The subnet mask on the server is incorrect
The DNS server is returning the wrong address
explanation: Ping succeeding proves routing and Layer 3 reachability are intact, so the failure is selective by port — the signature of an ACL or firewall rule. A gateway or mask error would break ping as well.

prompt: A router has no entry for a destination network and no default route configured. What happens to packets for that network?
choices: They are dropped, and the router may return an ICMP destination unreachable
They are flooded out every interface except the one they arrived on
They are queued until a matching route is learned
They are forwarded to the nearest broadcast address
explanation: Routers drop what they cannot match; unlike switches, they never flood. The ICMP destination unreachable returned to the source is often the first clue that a route is missing.

prompt: Two hosts are configured as 192.168.10.20/24 and 192.168.10.200/26. They cannot communicate reliably even though both are physically on the same segment. What is the cause?
choices: Mismatched subnet masks, so each host disagrees about which addresses are local
Duplicate IP addresses on the segment
A VLAN mismatch between the two switch ports
An expired DHCP lease on one of the hosts
explanation: With a /26, the second host believes the local subnet spans only 192.168.10.192 to 192.168.10.255, so it sends traffic for .20 to its gateway instead of directly. Communication may work in one direction and fail in the other, which is the classic asymmetric signature of a mask mismatch.

prompt: A workstation has a correct address and mask but a default gateway set to an address that does not exist on the subnet. What symptom results?
choices: Local communication works, but nothing beyond the subnet is reachable
The workstation cannot reach anything, including local hosts
The workstation receives an APIPA address instead
Only DNS resolution fails, while direct IP access works
explanation: Local traffic never touches the gateway, so it continues working normally. Anything requiring routing fails silently, since the host ARPs for a gateway that never answers.

prompt: A host can ping external IP addresses successfully but cannot resolve any hostnames, and the configured DNS server address is on a subnet that no longer exists. What is the fault?
choices: An incorrect DNS server setting on the client
A missing default gateway
An incorrect subnet mask
An exhausted DHCP scope
explanation: Successful pings by address prove routing works, isolating the problem to name resolution. Pointing at an unreachable resolver produces exactly this split between working IP connectivity and failing name lookups.

prompt: Two devices on a network are found to have been manually assigned the same IP address. What symptom is most characteristic?
choices: Intermittent connectivity for both hosts as ARP entries flip between them
Both hosts lose all connectivity permanently and immediately
Both hosts receive APIPA addresses
Traffic between the two hosts is silently encrypted
explanation: Other devices cache whichever MAC answered most recently, so traffic oscillates between the two hosts as their ARP entries compete. The intermittent, alternating nature of the symptom is what distinguishes it from a hard failure.

prompt: A cloned virtual machine and its source both come online and network connectivity for both becomes erratic, with switch logs reporting the same MAC address flapping between two ports. What is the cause?
choices: A duplicate MAC address between the two virtual machines
A duplicate IP address between the two virtual machines
A spanning tree loop between the hypervisor uplinks
An MTU mismatch on the virtual switch
explanation: Cloning without regenerating the virtual NIC address produces two hosts claiming one MAC, and the switch cannot keep a stable table entry for it. The MAC-flapping log message is the distinguishing clue, since duplicate IP problems appear at Layer 3 instead.

prompt: A laptop that worked yesterday now has no address after being left off overnight, and the DHCP server logs show no requests from it at all. Its switch port shows no link. Where should troubleshooting focus?
choices: The physical layer, since without link no DHCP request can be sent
The DHCP scope, which has likely been exhausted
The DNS configuration on the client
The default gateway configuration on the router
explanation: No link means nothing above Layer 1 can function, so DHCP, DNS, and gateway settings are all irrelevant until the link is restored. Working bottom-up here avoids a long detour through service configuration.

prompt: A file transfer between two sites achieves only a fraction of the circuit's rated speed, while latency measures 180 ms. Which factor most likely limits throughput?
choices: High latency limiting TCP throughput given the window size
Insufficient DHCP addresses on the remote subnet
An incorrect subnet mask on the receiving host
A VLAN mismatch on the WAN interface
explanation: TCP throughput is bounded by window size divided by round-trip time, so a long path throttles a single stream regardless of available bandwidth. Window scaling or parallel streams are the usual remedies for a high bandwidth-delay product.

prompt: Monitoring shows a WAN circuit consistently at 98 percent utilization during business hours, with rising queue drops. Which term best describes this condition?
choices: Congestion, where offered load exceeds available capacity
Jitter, where packet arrival times vary
Attenuation, where signal strength decreases over distance
Latency introduced by the routing protocol
explanation: Congestion is the condition where demand exceeds the link's capacity, and queue drops are its direct consequence. The practical responses are adding capacity or applying QoS so that important traffic is queued preferentially.

prompt: In a network path, one 100 Mbps link sits between several gigabit segments, and all traffic through that path is limited to roughly 100 Mbps. What is this link called?
choices: A bottleneck
A broadcast domain
A collision domain
A demarcation point
explanation: The slowest link in a path determines end-to-end throughput regardless of how fast the surrounding segments are. Identifying it is why hop-by-hop throughput testing is more useful than testing only the endpoints.

prompt: A voice call has consistent 40 ms latency, but users report choppy audio. Packet capture shows inter-arrival times varying between 5 ms and 90 ms. Which impairment is responsible?
choices: Jitter
Attenuation
Packet loss
Duplex mismatch
explanation: Jitter is variation in delay rather than delay itself, and it defeats the fixed-size buffers voice endpoints use to smooth playback. A larger jitter buffer helps at the cost of added latency, but QoS at the congested hop is the real fix.

prompt: A wireless client sits at the edge of coverage and repeatedly drops off the network and reconnects. Which condition describes this behaviour?
choices: Client disassociation caused by insufficient signal strength
Channel overlap between two adjacent access points
An SSID mismatch on the client
A DHCP scope exhaustion event
explanation: Once the signal falls below the threshold the radio needs, the client is disassociated and must reassociate when the signal recovers. The cycle repeats at the coverage edge, which is why survey-driven AP placement matters.

prompt: A user walking through a building keeps a connection to a distant access point at poor signal rather than moving to a nearer one with a strong signal. What is this behaviour called?
choices: Sticky client behaviour, a roaming misconfiguration issue
Band steering working as designed
Co-channel interference between the two access points
A captive portal timeout
explanation: Clients decide when to roam, and many hold an existing association well past the point where a better AP is available. Tuning minimum data rates and roaming-assist thresholds nudges clients to let go earlier.

prompt: A new Wi-Fi 6 access point is deployed, but an older laptop connects at only 54 Mbps and cannot use the wider channels. What explains this?
choices: An access point and client capability mismatch, since the laptop supports an older 802.11 standard
The access point is transmitting at too high a power level
The laptop is being rejected by MAC filtering
The SSID is hidden, forcing a slower connection
explanation: A client can only use the features its own radio implements, so an 802.11a or g client caps out at 54 Mbps regardless of the AP. Mixed environments also drag down overall cell performance, since legacy rates occupy more airtime per frame.

prompt: An office deploys many access points at maximum transmit power to maximize coverage, and performance gets worse rather than better. Why?
choices: Overlapping cells at high power increase co-channel interference and contention
High transmit power reduces the number of available SSIDs
High transmit power forces all clients onto the 2.4 GHz band
High transmit power disables channel bonding
explanation: Turning every radio up makes each cell larger, so more clients contend for the same airtime and hear more interference from neighbouring APs. Dense deployments perform better with lower power and smaller, well-separated cells.

prompt: Which command-line tool shows each router hop along the path to a destination along with the latency at each hop?
choices: traceroute or tracert
ping
netstat
arp
explanation: Traceroute maps the path by sending packets with incrementing TTL values and recording which router returns each Time Exceeded message. It reveals where in the path latency or loss begins, which a simple ping cannot.

prompt: A technician needs detailed DNS query output, including the authority and additional sections, from a specific name server. Which tool is best suited?
choices: dig
ping
netstat
arp
explanation: dig gives full, structured DNS output and lets you direct the query at a chosen server, which is essential when comparing what different resolvers return. nslookup is the more limited, though widely available, alternative.

prompt: Which command displays and allows manipulation of the local IP-to-MAC address mapping table?
choices: arp
route
netstat
nslookup
explanation: The arp command lists cached IP-to-MAC mappings and can delete stale entries, which is useful when a device has been replaced but traffic still follows the old hardware address. Clearing the entry forces a fresh resolution.

prompt: Which command displays the local routing table on a host, showing the default gateway and any static routes?
choices: route print on Windows, or ip route on Linux
arp -a on either platform
netstat -b on either platform
nslookup on either platform
explanation: The routing table shows exactly where the host will send traffic for each destination, which quickly settles questions about a wrong gateway or a leftover static route. On Linux the older equivalent is the route command.

prompt: A technician needs to capture and inspect packets from the command line on a Linux router with no graphical interface. Which tool is appropriate?
choices: tcpdump
nmap
nslookup
iperf
explanation: tcpdump captures live traffic with BPF filters and can write to a file for later analysis in a graphical analyzer. nmap probes for open ports rather than observing traffic in flight.

prompt: A technician wants to confirm whether a remote server is listening on TCP port 25 without installing new software on a Windows workstation. Which quick check can be used?
choices: Attempting a Telnet connection to the host on port 25
Running ipconfig /all on the workstation
Running arp -a against the server address
Pinging the server and observing the TTL
explanation: Telnet to an arbitrary port succeeds only if something is listening and reachable, which makes it a fast reachability test for a single port. Modern equivalents include the PowerShell cmdlet Test-NetConnection and netcat on Unix systems.

prompt: Which tool is used to identify wireless channel utilization, overlapping networks, and signal strength across a coverage area?
choices: A Wi-Fi analyzer
A tone generator and probe
A time domain reflectometer
A protocol analyzer on a wired span port
explanation: A Wi-Fi analyzer surveys the RF environment, showing which channels are congested and how neighbouring networks overlap. A spectrum analyzer goes further and reveals non-802.11 interference that a Wi-Fi analyzer cannot see.

prompt: What advantage does a passive network tap have over a switch port mirror for capturing traffic?
choices: It cannot drop frames under load and does not consume switch resources
It can capture traffic from any VLAN on the switch without configuration
It automatically decrypts TLS sessions for inspection
It requires no physical access to the cable path
explanation: A mirror port competes for switch resources and silently drops frames when the aggregate source traffic exceeds the destination port's capacity. A tap sits inline in the physical path and is therefore unaffected by switch load, at the cost of requiring a cable break to install.

prompt: A technician needs to determine whether an internal link can actually sustain its rated throughput between two hosts. Which tool is designed for this measurement?
choices: iperf, which generates traffic between a client and server endpoint
arp, which resolves addresses on the local segment
nslookup, which queries DNS records
tracert, which maps hops along a path
explanation: iperf generates controlled TCP or UDP streams and measures achieved throughput, jitter, and loss between two endpoints. Testing against an internet speed test measures the internet path instead, which is a different question.

prompt: Which tool identifies which physical cable in a bundle corresponds to a known end, by injecting an audible signal onto the conductor?
choices: A tone generator and inductive probe
A cable certifier
An optical power meter
A loopback plug
explanation: The toner injects a signal at one end and the probe finds it at the other by induction, without needing to connect to both ends simultaneously. A certifier instead measures whether an installed run meets its category specification.

prompt: A newly installed fiber link shows a receive level of minus 28 dBm against a transceiver minimum of minus 20 dBm. What does this indicate?
choices: Excessive optical loss in the link, from dirty connectors, tight bends, or excessive length
That the transmitter is over-driving the receiver
That the wrong VLAN is configured on the port
That the fiber pairs are reversed between TX and RX
explanation: A receive level below the transceiver's sensitivity means too much light is being lost along the path. Dirty or damaged connectors are the most common cause by a wide margin, which is why cleaning is always the first step.

prompt: After a switch is replaced, a group of users lose access to a server they previously reached, while other users on the same switch are unaffected. What should be checked first?
choices: The VLAN assignments on the affected users' ports
The DNS records for the server
The DHCP lease duration on the scope
The server's disk capacity
explanation: A partial failure that follows a hardware swap almost always traces to configuration that did not carry over, and port VLAN assignment is the most common omission. That other users are unaffected rules out anything shared, like the uplink or the server itself.

prompt: A network experiences a broadcast storm, and switch CPU utilization spikes to 100 percent across several devices. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A Layer 2 loop where spanning tree is disabled or has failed
A duplicate IP address on the management VLAN
An exhausted DHCP scope
An MTU mismatch on the core uplinks
explanation: Without spanning tree, a redundant Layer 2 path lets broadcasts circulate endlessly, multiplying with each pass. The traffic saturates links and CPUs network-wide, which is why the symptom rarely stays confined to one switch.

prompt: Spanning tree recalculates repeatedly across a network, causing brief outages every few minutes. Investigation shows a switch under a user's desk has a lower bridge priority than the intended root. What has happened?
choices: An unauthorized switch has become the root bridge, destabilizing the topology
The core switch has exhausted its MAC address table
A duplex mismatch is generating late collisions
The access ports are missing their voice VLAN assignment
explanation: Spanning tree elects the lowest bridge ID as root, so any switch introduced with a better priority takes the role and reshapes the topology around itself. Root guard on access ports prevents this by rejecting superior BPDUs.

prompt: A trunk between two switches carries VLANs 10 and 20 correctly, but VLAN 30 traffic never passes. What should be checked?
choices: Whether VLAN 30 is in the allowed VLAN list on the trunk and exists on both switches
Whether the trunk ports have PortFast enabled
Whether the DHCP scope for VLAN 30 has free addresses
Whether the trunk is using the correct duplex setting
explanation: Trunks carry only the VLANs they are permitted to carry, and a VLAN missing from the allowed list or absent from the VLAN database is silently dropped. That only one VLAN is affected rules out physical and duplex problems.

prompt: Users report the network is slow, and monitoring shows a single host generating tens of thousands of small packets per second to sequential addresses. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: A compromised host scanning or generating malicious traffic
A DHCP scope nearing exhaustion
An access point transmitting at excessive power
A misconfigured NTP client
explanation: Sequential-address, high-rate traffic from one host is the signature of scanning or worm propagation rather than normal application behaviour. Isolating that host is both a performance fix and a security response.

prompt: A branch site's users report that internal applications are fast but all internet browsing is slow, and the WAN link shows low utilization. Where should investigation focus next?
choices: The proxy or internet-facing security appliance handling outbound requests
The access switch's MAC address table size
The spanning tree topology within the branch LAN
The PoE budget on the branch switch
explanation: Internal traffic being healthy while only internet-bound traffic suffers points at the devices unique to that path, and low link utilization rules out congestion. A saturated proxy or inspection appliance is a common culprit.

prompt: After a change to a firewall rule set, one application breaks while everything else continues to work. What is the most efficient first diagnostic step?
choices: Review the change against the rule set, checking for a broad rule shadowing a specific one
Reboot the firewall to clear its state table
Replace the firewall with a spare unit
Increase the MTU on the firewall's inside interface
explanation: A fault that appears immediately after a change and affects only one flow is almost always caused by that change, and rule ordering is the usual mechanism. Rebooting or swapping hardware discards evidence and is disproportionate to the symptom.

prompt: A remote user's VPN connects successfully, but they cannot reach any internal resource by name while IP addresses work. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The VPN is not pushing internal DNS servers or the correct search suffix to the client
The VPN tunnel is using the wrong encryption algorithm
The user's account lacks permission to establish the tunnel
The client's default gateway is missing entirely
explanation: A working tunnel with functioning IP reachability isolates the fault to name resolution, and split-tunnel configurations frequently leave the client using its home resolver. Pushing internal DNS servers and suffixes to the client resolves it.

prompt: Only some websites fail to load over a newly established site-to-site VPN, and the failures correlate with pages containing large images. Smaller pages work. What should be adjusted?
choices: The MTU or MSS on the tunnel, to account for encapsulation overhead
The DNS server assigned to the remote subnet
The DHCP lease duration at the remote site
The spanning tree priority on the remote switch
explanation: Tunnel headers reduce the space available for payload, so full-size packets exceed the path MTU and are dropped when fragmentation is blocked. Lowering the MTU or clamping the TCP MSS on the tunnel interface is the standard fix.

prompt: A technician replaces a suspected faulty patch cable with a known-good one and the problem disappears. Which troubleshooting technique is this?
choices: Substitution with a known-good component
Divide and conquer
Top-down analysis
Baseline comparison
explanation: Substitution isolates a fault by swapping one variable at a time for a component known to work. Its value depends on changing only one thing, since swapping several at once leaves you unable to say which was responsible.

prompt: Users complain that a service is intermittently unavailable, but the technician cannot reproduce it. What is the most productive next step?
choices: Gather data on when it occurs, correlating user reports with monitoring and logs
Reboot the servers involved during business hours
Replace the network equipment along the path
Close the ticket as unable to reproduce
explanation: Intermittent faults are solved by finding the pattern — time of day, specific users, specific paths — and correlating it with recorded data. Acting before the pattern is established usually changes the symptom without fixing the cause.

prompt: A switch interface counter shows a rising number of giants. What does this indicate?
choices: Frames are arriving larger than the configured MTU for the interface
Frames are arriving smaller than the 64-byte minimum
The interface is dropping frames because its buffers are full
The interface has negotiated half duplex
explanation: Giants exceed the interface's maximum frame size, which usually means one side has jumbo frames enabled and the other does not. Runts are the opposite condition and typically indicate collisions or a faulty transmitter.

prompt: A user reports that they lose network connectivity every few days and it returns after they reboot. The workstation uses DHCP with a three-day lease. What should be investigated?
choices: Whether the DHCP lease is failing to renew, leaving the client without a valid address
Whether the workstation's subnet mask is incorrect
Whether the switch port has PortFast disabled
Whether the default gateway is missing from the scope options
explanation: A failure whose interval matches the lease period points directly at renewal, since a reboot forces a fresh DHCP exchange that temporarily restores service. Renewal failures often trace to a relay agent or an unreachable server rather than the client.

prompt: Which condition would cause a host to receive a valid IP address but still be unable to reach any host on any other subnet, while the gateway itself responds to ping?
choices: An access control list on the router blocking transit traffic from that subnet
An incorrect DNS server address on the host
A duplicate MAC address on the local segment
An exhausted DHCP scope on the router
explanation: Reaching the gateway proves local connectivity and correct gateway configuration, so the block is happening at the router as it forwards. An ACL applied in the wrong direction or missing a needed permit produces exactly this.

prompt: A monitoring alert reports that a core switch's uptime has reset to a few minutes, with no change ticket recorded. What should the technician check first?
choices: The device logs and power source, to determine whether it crashed or lost power
The DNS records pointing at the switch's management address
The DHCP scope serving the management VLAN
The spanning tree cost on each access port
explanation: An unexplained reset is either a software crash or a power event, and the device log plus the UPS log distinguish the two quickly. Establishing which one occurred determines whether the next step is a firmware investigation or an electrical one.

prompt: Users report that voice calls sound choppy and words drop out, while file transfers over the same link are unaffected. Which TWO measurements should be examined first?
choices: Jitter, the variation in packet arrival times
Packet loss along the path carrying the voice traffic
The DHCP lease duration configured on the voice VLAN
The MAC address table size on the access switch
The DNS resolution time for the call server's hostname
explanation: Voice is far more sensitive to jitter and loss than bulk transfers are, which is exactly why one degrades while the other looks fine. TCP simply retransmits what it loses, so a link can be unusable for calls while file copies still complete.

prompt: A fiber link between two switches will not come up. Which TWO causes should be checked first?
choices: A transceiver mismatch in wavelength or fiber type between the two ends
Dirty or damaged connector end faces on the patch cables
An incorrect DHCP scope on the management VLAN
An expired TLS certificate on the switch web interface
A missing DNS record for the far-end switch
explanation: Optics that do not match and contaminated end faces account for the large majority of fiber links that fail to establish. Addressing, certificates, and DNS all operate above a link that does not yet exist.

prompt: Which TWO symptoms together most strongly suggest a duplex mismatch on a copper link?
choices: Late collisions counted on the half-duplex side
Throughput far below the negotiated link speed
The port failing to establish link at all
The port receiving frames larger than the configured MTU
The switch reporting the same MAC address on two ports
explanation: A duplex mismatch still establishes link, which is what makes it easy to miss — the giveaways are late collisions and throughput that collapses under load. No link at all is a physical problem, and MAC flapping indicates a duplicate address or a loop.

prompt: Which TWO tools would help determine why an installed copper run fails certification?
choices: A cable certifier that measures the run against its category specification
A time domain reflectometer to locate the distance to a fault
A protocol analyzer capturing application traffic
An optical power meter measuring receive levels
A Wi-Fi analyzer surveying channel usage
explanation: Certification failures are physical-layer problems, so the tools must measure the cable itself: a certifier judges compliance and a TDR pinpoints where the fault is. Optical meters apply to fiber, and the other two operate well above Layer 1.

prompt: Users on one floor report slow wireless while the wired network performs normally. Which TWO causes are most plausible?
choices: Co-channel interference from access points reusing the same channel
A non-802.11 interference source raising the noise floor on that floor
An exhausted DHCP scope serving the entire building
A duplex mismatch on the building's core uplink
An expired certificate on the wireless controller's web interface
explanation: The problem being wireless-only and floor-specific points at the RF environment in that area. A building-wide DHCP issue or a core uplink fault would affect wired users too.

prompt: Which TWO conditions would cause a DHCP client to fail to obtain an address on a remote subnet?
choices: No DHCP relay agent or helper address configured on the router interface
The DHCP scope for that subnet having no free addresses remaining
An incorrect DNS suffix configured in the scope options
A lease duration set longer than 24 hours
The client having a static route to the DHCP server
explanation: DHCP discovery is broadcast and does not cross a router without a relay, and a scope with no free addresses has nothing to offer. Suffixes and lease durations affect what a client receives, not whether it receives anything.

prompt: A technician needs to prove whether packet loss on a path is occurring inside the corporate network or beyond the ISP handoff. Which TWO approaches provide that evidence?
choices: Running a continuous path analysis tool such as pathping or mtr to see loss per hop
Testing to the ISP's first hop and comparing loss against tests to a destination beyond it
Checking the DHCP scope utilization on the local subnet
Reviewing the DNS resolution time for the destination hostname
Verifying the certificate chain presented by the destination server
explanation: Per-hop loss statistics and a comparison of near versus far test points both localize where loss begins. Addressing, name resolution, and certificates are unrelated to packet loss along a path.

prompt: Which TWO conditions on a switch would cause frames from one VLAN to be delivered into a different VLAN?
choices: A native VLAN mismatch between the two ends of a trunk
An access port assigned to the wrong VLAN
PortFast enabled on an access port
Jumbo frames enabled on the uplink
An access control list applied to a routed interface
explanation: Untagged native VLAN traffic landing in a different VLAN at the far end, and a port simply configured for the wrong VLAN, are the two straightforward ways traffic ends up somewhere it should not be. PortFast and jumbo frames affect timing and frame size, not VLAN membership.

prompt: A host on VLAN 10 opens a connection to a server on VLAN 20 by hostname, with the two VLANs routed by a Layer 3 switch. Place these events in the order they occur.
items: The host queries its DNS server and receives the server's IP address
The host compares the destination against its own subnet mask and decides the target is remote
The host ARPs for its default gateway and builds a frame addressed to the gateway's MAC
The Layer 3 switch routes the packet from the VLAN 10 interface to the VLAN 20 interface
The switch ARPs for the destination host on VLAN 20 and delivers the frame
explanation: Tracing this sequence is what lets you place a failure precisely: a name that will not resolve fails at step one, while a host that resolves fine but cannot reach the gateway fails at step three. Note that the destination MAC changes at each routed hop while the IP addresses stay the same end to end.

prompt: A user reports that a workstation cannot reach an internal web server. Place these diagnostic checks in a sensible bottom-up order.
items: Confirm the switch port shows link and the cable is seated
Confirm the workstation has a valid IP address, mask, and gateway
Ping the default gateway to confirm local Layer 3 reachability
Ping the web server by IP address to confirm routing
Resolve the web server's hostname to confirm DNS is working
Connect to the server's port to confirm the service is listening
explanation: Bottom-up moves from the physical link upward, so each successful check narrows what remains. Reaching the server by address but not by name, for instance, isolates the fault to DNS without touching anything below it.

prompt: Type the Windows command that displays the local ARP cache, showing IP-to-MAC address mappings.
explanation: arp -a lists the cached IP-to-MAC mappings the host is using for local delivery. When a device has been replaced but traffic still follows the old hardware address, deleting the stale entry with arp -d forces a fresh resolution.

prompt: Type the Windows command that releases the current DHCP lease on all adapters.
explanation: ipconfig /release surrenders the current lease, and ipconfig /renew requests a new one. The pair is the standard way to force a client to re-run DHCP after a scope or reservation change.

prompt: Type the Windows command that pings the address 10.0.0.1 continuously until it is manually interrupted.
explanation: The -t switch makes Windows ping run without a count limit, which is how you watch for the brief drops that characterize an intermittent fault. Ctrl+Break prints running statistics without stopping it, and Ctrl+C ends the run.
